text:
We scanned 3.5 million hosts for exposed .git repos and walked away with 400 AWS keys
Leaving a .git directory exposed is an old mistake with a single well known path, so we wanted to know how many organisations still make it. We pulled hostnames from certificate transparency logs, scanned 3.5 million live hosts, and found 28,000 repositories sitting wide open. 

400 AWS access keys came out of them, including one with access to a bucket of internal employment records, attendance logs and disciplinary files. Many of the credentials we pulled were still active when we tested. We disclosed them where we could find a contact.

Tom Steer, one of our security consultants, wrote up what we found and how gitreaper works, the tool we built to walk a repo's whole commit history in memory rather than writing 28,000 repositories to disk. That's also why we caught secrets in files that had been removed in later commits, which is often where the worst of it is.

Exposed .git is one of many thousands of issues that could be sitting on the internet waiting for someone to find them. We write custom Nuclei checks for that sort of thing and report them as vulnerabilities in Intruder, so it turns up in your scan results with the remediation advice attached.

Full write-up: We found 28,000 .git repos sitting wide open. Here's what was inside

text:
With AI changing data engineering and app dev, what should I learn deeply, learn enough to get by, or skip entirely?
TL;DR: I'm an analytics engineer with about 3 years experience in data and with a mechanical engineering degree. My skills are spread across data engineering, app dev, and a little data science, without having deep knowledge in any of them. I want to know what’s actually worth learning now, how deep to go, and whether I should specialize.

How I got here

I studied mechanical engineering (aerospace emphasis), but I was always the tech kid: Java Minecraft mods, jailbroken iPhones, a few websites for local businesses. After some unenjoyable manufacturing engineering internships, I took a Python data analytics course and found a role that combined both worlds.

That first job was smart manufacturing at a tool company. I collected machine sensor data (Kepware, OSI PI, SQL Server) and tried ML models to predict machine damage and part quality. Those never reached production because the data was too noisy and failures were too rare. What did work was real-time dashboards for shop floor KPIs like OEE and run rate. Eventually I got tired of crawling around machines debugging PLCs, so I moved to the data side full time.

What I do now

I'm an analytics engineer on our supply chain team. I pull data from upstream warehouses and model it into star schemas that feed Power BI reports, Databricks dashboards, and Genie rooms. Most of the work is SQL. The business logic is full of exceptions, so some transformations run over 1,000 lines. Pipelines run in Databricks and ADF, and code goes through Azure DevOps (GitHub for apps) CI/CD pipelines.

My team is now building internal apps with React, Express, TypeScript, and Databricks AppKit. One experienced developer set up the framework, and the rest of us are mostly vibe coding on top of it.

On the side, I've taken full-stack courses and built two web games: a multiplayer name guessing game and a daily game where users solve color nonograms.

Where I stand

text:
Software engineer job postings ask for mentoring more than Kubernetes. We counted 3,518 postings to check
We pulled every open posting from 81 companies' public Greenhouse boards for seven roles and counted which words actually show up. 3,518 postings in total. Some of it surprised us.

Software engineer postings mention mentoring more often than Kubernetes or React. Almost half of them do. Python, the most common language, comes in just below that.

Product manager postings say "roadmap" in more than 85% of cases. Jira? Seven out of 421. Marketing looks the same: Google Ads came up six times in 347 postings, while "pipeline" is in over half.

Every time we could compare the two, postings named the practice, not the tool. Observability, not Grafana. SIEM, not Splunk.

So if your resume is mostly a list of tools, it might be missing the words the posting actually uses.

Big caveat: mostly tech companies, one ATS vendor. Sales, cybersecurity, DevOps and accounting are here too: https://www.zoevera.com/resume/ats-resume-keyword-study

Body:

Hi everyone,
I graduated with a B.S. in Computer Science (high GPA) and have ~1 year of dev experience.

I recently joined a well-regarded, structured company for a position pitched as leading into software development. Once I started, project leads made it clear: the role is 100% manual QA (writing test plan documents, clicking through the app, logging bugs). Test automation was framed as a vague "nice-to-have" if I figure it out myself and architect it alone, but our tech stack is notoriously painful for automation, and the dev team already tried and abandoned it. There are no production coding tasks for me.

A few experienced devs outside my immediate team told me not to throw in the towel—they argue that being inside a mature organization with Agile/Jira/sprints offers valuable lessons, that I can reframe the experience on my resume, and that patience might pay off.

My dilemma is choosing between two flawed options:

Stay in the new QA role: 20-min commute, low stress, structured processes, and a reputable brand name on paper. But the work is completely mindless manual clicking with a massive risk of getting pigeonholed as a tester.

Transfer back to my previous role: I was essentially a solo dev acting like an in-house freelancer—zero other software developers, no tech team, no code reviews, and no mentorship. The daily commute is brutal. However, I was writing code and building end-to-end applications every day while applying elsewhere for proper engineering roles.

Questions:
Does staying in manual QA for the "structure and brand name" hurt my chances of getting hired as a SWE later?

Is writing code as a completely isolated solo dev with no team still viewed more favorably by hiring managers than doing manual testing in a structured enterprise?

For those who started in manual testing, did you successfully pivot into dev, or did hiring managers treat it as a dead end?

text:
Could `shuf -n 100` outperform your ATS? I'd genuinely love someone with hiring data to test this.
Meta
TL;DR: Research suggests years of previous work experience barely predict job performance (r ≈ 0.07). So here's my hypothesis: randomly selecting 100 applicants out of 1,000 might be almost as effective as filtering them through an ATS, at a fraction of the cost and with fewer built-in biases. I can't test this without real hiring data. Can someone who has access to it try? I'd genuinely love to be proven wrong.

I've been looking into research on the predictive validity of hiring criteria, and stumbled upon something that I find both fascinating and slightly hilarious.

A 2019 meta-analysis by Van Iddekinge et al., covering 81 independent samples, found that previous work experience had a correlation of roughly 0.06 with subsequent job performance. Even relevant previous experience had a correlation of about 0.07.

Now, correlation isn't predictive accuracy, and those numbers don't mean that experience is entirely useless. But they're remarkably close to zero.

Which got me thinking.

Suppose you have 1,000 applicants for an engineering position, and you can afford to evaluate 100 of them.

Your ATS filters by years of experience, perhaps alongside other résumé criteria, and selects 100 candidates.

I propose a competing implementation:

shuf -n 100 applicants.txt
That's it.

If years of previous experience have almost no predictive relationship with actual job performance, then selecting candidates based on that criterion should offer very little advantage over random sampling.

And random sampling has some rather attractive properties:

Computational cost is effectively zero.

No elaborate infrastructure or language models required.

No arbitrary preference for prestigious employers, uninterrupted careers, or people who've spent exactly seven years writing Java.

No systematic discrimination introduced by the selection rule itself (though existing biases in the applicant pool remain).

Everyone eligible has a chance to be evaluated.

Of course, I'm talking about using random sampling instead of weakly predictive résumé filters, not instead of assessing candidates. Hard requirements that are genuinely necessary for the job can still be checked.

And there's a distinction worth making: ATS products do more than filter by experience, and this research doesn't establish the validity of every possible ATS configuration. My hypothesis concerns systems that rely heavily on years of experience and similar résumé proxies.

Here's the experiment I'd love somebody to run.

Take 1,000 real applications. Apply your normal screening process and select 100 candidates. Independently draw another 100 at random from the same eligible applicant pool.

Have both groups undergo the same blinded, job-relevant technical assessment.

Compare:

How many candidates meet the assessment threshold?

How many strong candidates did the conventional filter exclude?

How much did each method cost?

Does conventional screening provide enough additional value to justify its complexity and cost?

Ideally, we'd eventually compare actual job performance too, although that would require a more involved study. Passing a technical assessment is only a proxy.

I don't have access to hiring datasets, so I can't run this myself.

But I'd be genuinely curious whether someone in recruiting, HR analytics, or an engineering organisation has access to the data and would be willing to test it.

I'm particularly interested in the economic question. Even if conventional screening performs slightly better than random selection, is that difference large enough to pay for the screening machinery?

We're currently discussing LLMs, AI-powered candidate ranking, intelligent ATS systems, and all sorts of elaborate hiring technology.

Meanwhile, I'm wondering whether we've established that the machinery we're trying to improve actually beats a random number generator by a useful margin.

Has anyone tested this against a random baseline? I'd love to see the results, including results that prove my hypothesis wrong.

Reference: Van Iddekinge et al. (2019), A Meta-analysis of the Criterion-related Validity of Prehire Work Experience, Personnel Psychology.

https://doi.org/10.1111/peps.12335

text:
Programming languages DO matter, just not necessarily for the reasons people think
Experienced
People often say "programming languages don't matter," meaning a good dev should be able to pick up anything. I agree—up to a point. But there's a big nuance people miss: how well do you actually know the domain?

Think of it this way:

If you’re a backend dev switching from Node to Go, you're learning new syntax, but you already know how APIs work. It's an easy transition.

If you’re a Node dev staying in TypeScript but switching to infrastructure automation, you already know the language, so you can focus entirely on learning the new domain.

But if you’re a Node dev switching to Go for infrastructure work, you're learning the syntax, the domain, and the tools all at once. That's a massive hurdle. It's like trying to cross greased monkey bars.

The ramp-up time is way longer when you're learning both the language and the concepts, which is why I don't buy the blanket "languages don't matter" claim.

What about AI? Some say it makes the language irrelevant since it can write code for you. AI is great for syntax, but if you don't understand the domain, how can you even tell if the code it's giving you is actually good? Just because it runs doesn't mean it's the right way to build it.

AI can help you write code, but it doesn't automatically mean you know how to check if that code is right.

My main point:

I think developers need some kind of solid foundation to start with.

If the language is new, knowing the concepts helps.

If the concepts are new, knowing the language helps.

But if both are new, the learning curve gets a lot steeper.

I'm not saying developers can't learn a new language and a new domain at the same time. Obviously, they can.

I'm saying employers need to account for that extra learning time instead of expecting the same productivity and onboarding speed as someone who already knows the language or the domain.

So maybe "programming languages don't matter" is a bit of an oversimplification.

Maybe a better way to put it is:

"Programming languages matter less when the underlying concepts are familiar."

I'm curious what other engineers think. Have you ever had to jump into a project where both the language and the domain were new to you? How did that affect how long it took to get up to speed?

text:
Got my first software developer position
I haven't been on this sub for quite a while, but I remember most people being very worried for their future in technology due to the saturation of the job field and rise of AI.

I also was very worried for my future. I had invested many years of my life and debt to get a CS degree well into my 30s just for the market to become ultra competitive. Of course I got my degree while working full time so I never had internships or projects to speak of.

I finally finished my degree after like six years and got a promotion to help desk technician at the manufacturing company I was working at. I have been working that position for the last year and half and was just informed that they have promoted me to 'Full Stack Engineer'.

The company was implementing a warehouse management system to integrate with our ERP system and I saw the holes in the project and rushed in to fill them. I wrote two major pieces of software for the company that are being used on a daily basis including our automated order release system and a shipping app for our non-stocked items that ERP doesn't touch. I was informed if it were not for my efforts that the project would've not launched.

My recommendation to anyone with zero IT experience is to take the first best offer that you can get and demonstrate your capabilities within that role. At the time, I was just happy that I could get any tech related job at all, even if it was help desk. My resume is worst resume on this sub, so it was a blessing to just get that help desk job. I nearly got kicked out of school multiple times.

The leap from help desk to full stack engineer required a lot of effort as you may suspect. I worked many weekends, provided after hours support, led meetings, and made critical decisions. We just went live with our project and my software has already released thousands of orders and shipped hundreds of packages.

Prior to this position, I was a lead for a different department and I worked other stressful jobs over the years. That's the thing, I am coming into this at the age of 34 and many of you are in your early 20s and lack the soft skills that employers are looking for. The most important experience you can bring to a job are critical thinking and soft skills. A lot of this comes down to experience and age - and that is okay. Go work a help desk job, get some certs, become a sys admin, and get experience that life throws at you.

I am going from an overpaid help desk to an underpaid full stack engineer. 64k -> 71k (with 8% yearly bonus). HCOL area where median for full stack engineer is 125k. But you know what this doesn't bother me in the slightest and I am more than happy to gain the experience and build my salary over the years. As long as I work as hard as I have over the years, things will work in my favor.

Anyway, I hope this provides some inspiration to anyone feeling down about their job prospects. Let me know if you have any questions.

text:
Statistical rises in PR counts in the AI era are actually nonsense
Let me explain. My org heavily pressured us to get PR counts up. So, engineers did that by splitting up work into smaller items. It's actually more work --more context switching-- to review 2 smaller items than one item that is effectively the same thing.

We all know lines of code, PR counts, tickets closed are all proxies for actual productivity that moves businesses forward, and our work is too abstract to try and measure the real desired outcome (ostensibly: higher profits, more sales, etc) so they use this very rigid quantifiers.

text:
My job is making me question my abilities as a dev
Experienced
Hey everyone, I wanted to vent a little and get some outside perspectives on my current work situation.

TL;DR:
Dev with 5yoe, got moved to a new project just over a week ago with almost no onboarding. My manager thinks I'm underperforming and lacking autonomy, expecting me to find bugs, implement improvements, build dashboards, and deliver constantly. It's making me question my abilities and feel burned out.
Is this normal for a mid-level dev? How do you guys handle unfamiliar codebases? Should I try to improve my situation or start looking for another job?

Wall of text here:

I have around 5 years of experience as a developer and work at a fairly big company in my country. A little over a week ago, I was moved to a different team and project due to an internal reorganization.

My onboarding basically consisted of: "Clone this repo. It's yours now. Find bugs, fix them, and implement improvements." Since then, I've been analyzing the codebase using Codex, trying to understand how everything works.

Recently, my manager criticized my performance, saying I'm taking too long, lack autonomy, and that my performance is closer to a junior developer's than a mid-level's. He expects me to already be generating bug reports, fixing issues, building dashboards, and proactively identifying improvements.

I explained that I'm still getting familiar with the system and that parallelizing all these tasks after barely a week on the project is challenging.

We're also heavily encouraged to use AI for practically everything, which has been burning me out. I feel like there's more emphasis on producing output quickly than actually understanding what we're building.

What bothers me most is that I've never had my abilities questioned like this before. In previous jobs, I've built features end to end, deployed to production, worked with stakeholders, discussed about technical solutions with peers/leaders and handled tasks independently. I don't think I lack autonomy, I mean that I've never felt like I needed someone constantly holding my hand to get things done besides asking some questions to my manager/ seniors. I usually come with a solution and asks if its okay, i dont like going without anything and expect to get everything solved. but I do need some time to understand a project before I can confidently suggest improvements.

Now I feel like nothing I do is enough, and it's honestly making me question my abilities as a developer.

I'm also curious about how you approach unfamiliar codebases

my usual workflow is to explain the task and context to AI, propose an approach, and iterate on its suggestions until I fully understand and agree with the solution. Sometimes I wonder if I'm spending too much time trying to understand things instead of just implementing them.

So, a few questions:

Are these reasonable expectations for a mid level developer after just one week?

How do you approach understanding an unfamiliar codebase with AI? Am I being inefficient?

Would you try to turn this situation around or start looking for another job?

For context, I have 5 years of experience, mainly with React, Node.js, TypeScript, and .NET. I'm considering looking elsewhere, but I'm unsure how difficult finding another job would be in the current market

Application Support: Not sure how to move forward
I was a software engineer for a few years until I was laid off. It took me years to get my current role, which is Application Support. This job is very stable, and my finances are slowly recovering so I'm not keen to leave it anytime soon. Plus, this job is unionized, which I value very highly.

My org doesn't have any in-house development. It typically uses contractors to develop apps or systems and once the app is dev complete, it's passed to us to maintain, and the contractors go away. If we are ever still in contact with the contractors, often getting useful information from them is like pulling teeth because they have a financial disincentive to help us out.

We're typically (but not always!) trained on how to do extremely simple things like resetting passwords. Then we'll get a request to make some major change that requires some technical deep dive and there's no one with the knowledge we need to turn to for support.

The odd thing is: the org values training very much. They will pay to have experts from some software tool we use to give demonstrations or have regular "office hours" so we can learn how to use their software. However, obviously they can't tell us what our org's needs are or what we need to do with their tools. Management just gets angry at us when something goes wrong we had no way of anticipating.

I've talked with management about my concerns but their perception is basically: we spend all this money and time and effort on training, if you can't figure it out, it's on you. They do not think that Operational or Domain knowledge is a thing.

Lately, management has decided they want to bring development in-house. At first I liked this, because it's closer to the type of work I enjoy, but I'm getting increasingly nervous about it. We only very recently obtained access to AI, and I'm afraid management will expect AI to patch over any skill gaps we have. I am also the only person on my team with any recent software development experience (such as it was...), so I'm worried that it will fall on me to train the rest of the team to create mature development processes.

I feel like this could either be a great opportunity for me to grow, or a tremendous disaster. I'd like some guidelines or strategies to navigate this situation and do what I can to realistically improve things or at least keep my sanity.

text:
19, working at a Big 4 but want to become a SWE. Stay another 5 months or switch ASAP before university?

TL;DR: I'm 19, from Italy, working in IT Risk at a Big 4 (€25k/year). I've been programming since I was 12 and want to become a SWE, ideally in fintech. I'm definitely starting a CS degree in September 2027, so I'm wondering whether to stay at my current job until July or start applying aggressively for SWE positions. I'd also appreciate an honest assessment of how competitive my profile is in today's market.

P.s. big4 as in Deloitte, KPMG, PwC, EY

My background
I graduated from a technical high school specializing in IT this June. I've been programming for around seven years, and some of my recent open-source projects include:

A banking backend with a double-entry ledger, account management and transaction processing.

A cryptographic timestamping service with a deployed backend, public API and working demo.

I mainly use Java, Python and TypeScript (Spring Boot, Node.js, PostgreSQL). I also solve at least one LeetCode problem daily and regularly experiment with AI coding tools.

I genuinely love software engineering, although I know personal projects aren't a substitute for professional experience.

My current situation
I joined a Big 4 in September. The environment is fantastic, my colleagues are great, and the workload is relatively relaxed.

However, most of my work involves IT controls, compliance and auditing. I'm learning how large organizations operate, but the technical work feels repetitive, and I'm barely using my programming skills.

My contract ends in February 2027, but a further five-month extension is practically guaranteed. I could therefore stay until July and have almost a year of Big 4 experience on my resume.

University and my dilemma
Starting a Computer Science degree in September 2027 is non-negotiable. I was already accepted at Milano-Bicocca this year but postponed enrollment to take the job.

I currently work 9–6 with two hours of daily commuting, so combining this schedule with university isn't realistic for me. I want to actually learn the material, not just pass exams.

Fortunately, I don't depend on my salary for basic living expenses. It's great for savings, independence and my limited social life, but career development matters more.

I'm considering two options:

A) Stay at the Big 4 until July, save money, gain corporate experience and then focus on university.

B) Start applying aggressively for junior SWE/backend roles and internships in November, even accepting a pay cut. Ideally, I'd find something that could become part-time during university.

Long-term, I'm aiming for a product-focused SWE career, preferably in fintech. Finance genuinely interests me, particularly banking and payment infrastructure, so combining both fields would be ideal. I'm also open to relocating internationally and want to aim high professionally.

What I'd like advice on
Was postponing university by a year for a Big 4 job a mistake? Does IT Risk experience at a recognizable company carry meaningful weight for SWE recruiters, particularly in fintech, where financial systems, controls and compliance matter?

Would you take the additional five-month contract or try to switch to SWE ASAP? Is a few months of actual development experience more valuable than almost a year at a Big 4, considering university starts in September regardless?

How competitive is my profile realistically? At 19, without a degree but with seven years of programming, public backend projects and some corporate experience, would I be worth interviewing for junior SWE roles? How do I compare with CS students?

What would you prioritize before September 2027? SWE experience, improving projects, interview preparation, or simply staying employed and saving money?

I genuinely like my current job and the people I work with. I'm just concerned about getting comfortable in a career I don't want long-term.

If you were in my position, what would you do? I'd particularly appreciate honest feedback from engineers or hiring managers about my chances in the current market.
